subject: Copywriting
title: Dave Trott: Creative Mischief
description: Learn Dave Trott: Creative Mischief in one minute.

hook.text: Dave Trott says 90% of advertising is invisible. Nobody remembers it. The only crime in advertising is being boring.

buildup.text: Trott worked in London's creative scene and wrote books distilling advertising wisdom into short, punchy stories.

discovery.text: His framework: impact, then communication, then persuasion.

twist.text: Trott argues that data-driven advertising has made everything safe—and therefore invisible. Creativity requires risk.

climax.text: His books 'Creative Mischief' and 'One Plus One Equals Three' became cult reading for young creatives worldwide.

punchline.text: 90% of ads are invisible. Be the 10% people remember.

quiz.question: What does Trott say is the first requirement of advertising?

details.summary: Dave Trott is a British advertising legend who champions simplicity, impact, and what he calls 'predatory thinking.' His books — 'Creative Mischief,' 'Predatory Thinking,' and 'One Plus One Equals Three' — distill decades of creative strategy into short, punchy stories that teach by example.
details.whyItMatters: Trott cuts through the pretension of modern advertising theory with street-level wisdom. His emphasis on cutting through clutter is more relevant than ever in an attention-scarce digital world.
takeaways: He coined 'predatory thinking' as an approach to creative problem-solving
Trott argues that 89% of all advertising goes completely unnoticed
His writing uses short stories to teach advertising principles memorably

faq.question: What is predatory thinking?
faq.answer: Predatory thinking is Trott's framework for creative problem-solving. It means identifying the real problem (not the obvious one), finding an unexpected angle of attack, and executing with ruthless simplicity. It is thinking that hunts opportunities rather than waiting for them.

faq.question: Why does Trott say most advertising goes unnoticed?
faq.answer: He cites research showing that 89% of ads are neither noticed nor remembered. Most advertising fails not because it offends, but because it is invisible. Trott argues that impact — getting noticed at all — should be the first creative priority before everything else.
